title: Data Desk
description: Collect answers one at a time, set them out in a table under their names, turn a pictograph row into a number with its key, and find the most, the least, the same and the total.
modes: none. One flow, one phase at a time. The host mounts a phase (phase prop). With navigableDots true, or no phase, the child may jump phases with the dots (user mode); otherwise the dots show progress and the teacher agent drives window.toolApi (AI mode). The last phase, and a whole lesson, end on the summary page, where Free play and Play again sit.

stage.sizing: the frame is min(100vw, 177.78vh) wide and min(100vh, 56.25vw) tall (dvh where supported); the svg fills it. Nothing scrolls.

bands.header: 0 to 80. One line: the tool name, a measured dot, the phase concept; again, sound and restart as round controls far right.
bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded card holding the running count, the working area, the question, the answer box and the keypad; the summary page covers it at the end.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The mascot at the far left on its ground line, the speech bubble beside it, the phase dots and the phase and question counts at the right.

zones.controls: circles r 28 at cx 1388, 1460, 1532, cy 40: again, sound, restart; 72-unit finger boxes
zones.dots: one pill per phase across bar, pitch 158; in user mode each is a button with a 72-tall finger box

stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box on the stage. The score leaves on finished and onComplete and is shown once, as stars on the summary page.

writeup.why: Collect facts that give information, set them out in a table under their names, read a pictograph row with its key, and find the most, the least, the same and the total.
writeup.look: A desk with a drawn class along its top edge, a heap of answer slips, a ruled table in the middle, and a pictograph board that slides over it with a compare rail beside it.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only. 'Data Desk' sits in ink at the far left, with a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it. The phase title sits beside the dot on the same line, then the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart stand as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the answers collected, the slips placed, the symbols counted in the row being read, or the rows placed on the rail, against what this phase holds, two numbers in ink. The first climbs by one as each child answers, each slip lands, each symbol is counted or each row takes its place, and the second is fixed at what this phase holds. The symbols of a row are counted here and nowhere else. The row's number is written at the end of its row, so a count of pictures and the number it stands for never share a place. Nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The class row runs along the top of the working area: up to thirty drawn children, each 32 by 88 with 3 between, at 64,210, reaching 1111. The class is line drawing in near-black ink on the panel colour, so no child is mistaken for a symbol. A child who has answered carries a small tick at their feet and cannot be asked twice. Tapping a child drops their answer onto the desk as a slip, a card 96 by 36 with the answer's name on it. It lands in the slip heap, a tray 220 by 330 at 64,322. The table stands to the right of the heap: up to six heading cells, each 110 by 64, in a row at 300,330, and a number cell 110 by 72 under each at 300,394. The total cell, 130 by 136, stands at the table's end at 960,330. A slip dragged to a column slides under its heading, and the number in that column climbs by one in amber. The total cell adds the numbers under the headings and writes the sum in reddish purple. The check strip under the table, 790 by 56 at 300,482, stands the count of slips in the heap beside it. The total cell's label says answers, and it says children only when each child gave one answer. The pictograph board, 820 by 340 at 300,322, slides in over the table from the right. A title strip 620 by 44 runs along its top, and the key card stands at 930,322, 190 by 80, showing one symbol and what it stands for. Up to six rows stand below from 412, each 36 tall with 6 between. Each row has its name in a cell 130 wide at the left, then its symbols from 440, each 36 wide with 8 between, up to ten. Its number, with its unit, sits in a tag 90 wide just beyond its last symbol. Tapping a row lays the pale sky blue band behind it. The row reader then counts its symbols into the running count one at a time. It takes the key's value once under each symbol in amber, and the row's number lands in its tag. The compare rail runs under the board, 820 by 56 at 300,670, with up to six places for the rows' numbers, the largest at the left and the smallest at the right. Two equal numbers share one place, side by side under one near-black bracket. Tapping two numbers on the rail lights both rows on the board and lays the sky blue band behind the symbols by which the longer row passes the shorter. That stretch is counted and read with the key, and its size is written on the band. The total bar sits at the lower left, 220 by 56 at 64,670, and adds every row once when the question asks for all of them. Down the right of the canvas the question sits above the answer slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92), which holds what the child has given. That rectangle is the same on every phase and is never animated in or out. Under it is the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across wherever a count or a number is asked for. A word pad carries this desk's own words: the row names of the board or the table, and most, least, same, more and in all. The footer runs 758 to 900. The voice caption sits at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling. The phase bar sits at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own, taken from its pictures. Every upright tally mark is deep blue, and every fifth mark, drawn across the four before it, is vermilion. Every pictograph symbol, whole or half, in the key and in the rows, is green, except where the rows are named by colour. There each row's symbols wear that row's own colour: red, green, blue, yellow or purple. The key's symbol there is plain grey, which stands for one symbol of any colour and is used for nothing else. Amber is what a row, a column or a tally stands for once it is read, and so are the numbers in a table and the numbers a side ruler writes. Amber too is what half a symbol stands for, what a key leaves over, and a small round counter for one thing counted. A total of every row is reddish purple, and so is a thing a total counts more than once, such as a stop two routes share. The row a question asks about is marked by a pale sky blue band laid behind its symbols, never over them. So is the stretch by which one row or tally reaches beyond another. Chrome never borrows one of those, and none of them is ever used for chrome. Every table rule, row line, belt, route line, bracket, outlined blank and card edge is near-black, and titles, row names, headings and the wording of every key are near-black type. Every reading survives with the colour taken away. A fifth mark lies across and not upright, and a half symbol is the left half of the whole. A row's number sits beyond its end, a total sits in its own bar or cell, and a band lies behind a row rather than on it. No amount is ever drawn as a length of colour: an amount on this stage is symbols, marks, counters or a written number. A blank waiting for the child is an empty outlined box, never a faded copy of its answer. A count of symbols sits in the running count, and a row's number sits at its row's end. A sum of rows sits in the total cell or the total bar and nowhere else. The number a row stands for is never written in the corner, and a sum of rows is never written beside a single row.
writeup.finish: The card shows the table the child made from the answers they collected, with its total, and the pictograph rows standing on the compare rail in order.

phases.win: the last slip lands and the question card turns to show what the heap tells
phases.does: taps each child, watches the answer drop as a slip, then says what the heap of slips can tell the school
phases.goal: facts collected to give useful information are data, and each fact has a name that says what was counted
phases.says: Ask each child. What can all these answers tell the school?
phases.check: Away from the screen: ask five friends their favourite fruit. Write each answer down with its name.
phases.feels: each answer arrives with its name on it, one child at a time, and the heap grows by one
phases.hands: Before the tool is opened, ask the class how they came to school, and mark each answer on the board as it comes. Then write four numbers on the board with no names beside them, and ask what they tell anyone. Write the names back and ask again. The section headed Data Collection defines data and then only sets out data already collected, so let the class collect some first. Four numbers with no names tell nobody what was counted.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: what does each number count? Second rung, the phase's: what could the school learn from these answers? Third rung: the class is cut to three children, and the child collects their three slips and says what they tell. The word pad stays open behind all three rungs.

wrong.why: the numbers look just like the counts collected a minute ago, and a number seems to be the fact all by itself.
wrong.move: calls four numbers written with no names data about the class, and says what each one means.
wrong.screen: the four numbers stay on the desk as the child left them. The question card asks which of them is the bus. One at a time, each slip's name is drawn back beside its number, and the card is answered only once the names are back. Nothing is cleared.

wrong.why: weather reports are given as examples of data, and a picture of rain looks like part of one.
wrong.move: calls a drawing of a rain cloud data, because rain is in the weather reports the section names.
wrong.screen: the drawing is set beside the slip heap, and the question card asks how many. The heap answers with a count for each name. The drawing gives no count and no name, so nothing from it lands in the table, and it stays where the child put it.

wrong.why: a heap that grows looks like more data, and the child's answer is still a true answer.
wrong.move: taps a child who has already answered, to add their answer a second time.
wrong.screen: the child is drawn with the small tick at their feet and gives no second slip. The running count stays level with the children asked, and the heap stays as it was.

phases.screen: a drawn class along the top of the desk, an empty heap and a question card asking how each child came to school
phases.soWhat: Facts collected to give useful information are data, and each carries a name that says what was counted.

phases.win: the heap empties into the columns and the total cell matches the number of slips collected
phases.does: drags each slip into the column for its name, then fills the total cell
phases.goal: a table puts each number under its own name, and the numbers add up to the whole group
phases.says: Where does this answer belong? Now add the columns. Does the total match the heap?
phases.check: Four friends each pick one colour. Make a table. Does its total match the friends?
phases.feels: every slip slides under its own heading, and the columns add up to the heap they came from
phases.hands: Set the class's answers out on the board as a table, a heading for each way of coming to school and the number of children under it. Add the numbers, then count the children who were asked, and let the class see that the two match. Say why: each child gave one answer. Then ask each child for exactly two favourite games and add that table; its sum is twice the children. The chapter's own table heads its row team where the text says house, and lists the houses in another order. Every value agrees, so read it by the names.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: what name is on this slip? Second rung, the phase's: do the columns add up to the heap? Third rung: the heap is cut to five slips under two headings, and the child places each one and adds the two numbers. The number keys stay open.

wrong.why: the headings are the first thing in the table to count, and the numbers under them look like labels.
wrong.move: counts the headings instead of adding the numbers, and says there are four children because there are four seasons.
wrong.screen: the four heading cells are counted into the running count, and the child's four stays in the slot. The total cell then adds the numbers under them, six, nine, eight and five, one at a time, and twenty-eight lands. Each child chose one season, so the cell is labelled children, and the check strip stands the heap's twenty-eight slips beside it.

wrong.why: the columns stand close together, and the hand goes back to the column the last slip went into.
wrong.move: drops a slip into the column beside its name, so one column is one too many and its neighbour one too few.
wrong.screen: the column's slips fan out under their heading, each showing its name. The one whose name is not the heading's is lifted clear and turned so its name faces both headings. It stays where the child put it until the child moves it.

wrong.why: every total met so far has been the number of children, because every child so far gave one answer.
wrong.move: adds a table in which each child named two games, and calls the sum the number of children.
wrong.screen: the total cell matches the heap, twenty-four slips. The class row then shows its twelve children, each with two slips drawn from them, and the total cell's label reads answers, not children.

phases.screen: the heap of slips beside a ruled table with a heading for each answer and every number cell empty
phases.soWhat: A table puts each number under its own name, and its numbers add up to the children when each child gave one answer.
phases.concept: Setting data out in a table

phases.win: the key's value is taken once for each symbol and the row's number lands at the end of the row
phases.does: counts the symbols in the lit row, reads the key, and writes the row's number with its unit
phases.goal: a pictograph row is read by counting its symbols and taking the key that many times
phases.says: Count the pictures in this row. What does one picture stand for?
phases.check: One picture stands for four books. How many books do six pictures show?
phases.feels: each picture holds the same amount, and the row is that amount taken once for every picture
phases.hands: Draw one row of a pictograph on the board, five mango pictures, with a key of one picture for six mangoes. Ask how many mangoes, and wait for someone to say five. Then take the key once for each picture aloud: six, twelve, eighteen, twenty-four, thirty. The recap's pictograph of sixes has a key of one bat for three sixes, and its questions ask for sixes, not bats. So every row there is turned into sixes with the key before an answer is given.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: how many pictures are in the row? Second rung, the phase's: what does one picture stand for? Third rung: the row is cut to two symbols, and the child takes the key twice. The number keys stay open.

wrong.why: counting the pictures is the first thing done to a row, and the count looks like the answer.
wrong.move: writes the number of pictures as the answer, five mangoes, without using the key.
wrong.screen: the running count holds the five symbols. The row reader then takes the key's six once under each symbol in amber, climbing to thirty, which lands in the row's tag. The child's five stays in the slot beside it.

wrong.why: the rows are close together, and a finger sliding along a row can drift onto its neighbour.
wrong.move: reads the row above or below the one the question names.
wrong.screen: the lit row keeps its sky blue band. The row the child read is outlined, and its name is set beside the name the question gives. The row reader then counts the lit row's symbols one at a time.

wrong.why: the key card shows a number, and it is the only number printed anywhere near the row.
wrong.move: writes the key's own number, six, as the row's number.
wrong.screen: the row reader takes the six under the first symbol only and stops, with the tag reading six. It then carries on under each symbol in turn, and the tag climbs to thirty.

phases.screen: the pictograph board over the table, with its title strip and key card, and one row lit
phases.soWhat: A pictograph row is read by counting its symbols and taking the key that many times.
phases.concept: Reading a pictograph with its key

phases.win: the rows stand in order on the rail, two equal numbers level with each other, and the total fills the bar
phases.does: stands the rows on the compare rail, names the most, the least and the two that are equal, then taps the total bar
phases.goal: the most and the least come from comparing the numbers, and the total from adding every row once
phases.says: Which is the most? Which is the least? Which two are the same? Now add them all.
phases.check: Rows stand for eighteen, twelve and nine. Which is the least, and how many more is eighteen than nine?
phases.feels: the rows stand in order on the rail, and a difference is the stretch by which one row passes another
phases.hands: Read a pictograph with the class: which row is the most, which the least, and which two are the same. Then ask how many more one row has than another, and take the smaller from the larger. A question worded as how many children like one thing more than another means how many more chose it, so ask it that way. The recap asks how many sixes all five players hit together. There adding every row is what the question asks, and each six was hit by one player only.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which number is the largest? Second rung, the phase's: are two of the numbers the same? Third rung: the board is cut to two rows, and the child lines them up and counts the stars the longer row has left. The number keys and the word pad stay open.

wrong.why: adding every row is right for in all, and the stars are what the eye has been counting.
wrong.move: adds the stars, twenty-one, and gives that as the number of stickers in all.
wrong.screen: the running count holds the twenty-one stars. The total bar then adds the rows' numbers, twenty, thirty-two, twelve and twenty, and eighty-four lands in the bar. Each sticker was collected by one class, so the bar is labelled stickers in all. The child's twenty-one stays in the slot.

wrong.why: the question names two rows, and joining two numbers has always meant adding them.
wrong.move: adds the two numbers when the question asks how many more, giving forty-four for thirty-two and twelve.
wrong.screen: the two numbers are tapped on the rail and both rows light on the board. The sky blue band lies behind the five stars by which the longer row passes the shorter, and they are read with the key, twenty. The child's forty-four stays in the slot beside it.

wrong.why: the question names the first thing first, and its number is the one the eye finds.
wrong.move: answers a question worded as how many children like one thing more than another with the first thing's whole count.
wrong.screen: the question card turns to its other face, which asks how many more chose the first thing than the second. The two rows are lined up on the board, and the stretch by which the first passes the second is banded and counted.

phases.screen: the pictograph board with every row's number written, the compare rail empty and the total bar waiting
phases.soWhat: Read the most, the least and the same from the numbers. How many more is the smaller taken from the larger.
phases.concept: Most, least, equal and in all

writeup.delight: The second phase, once the total cell matches the heap. The children in the class row give a small wave one at a time from the left. Each waves as their own slip is found in its column and lights there for a moment. A child who gave two answers waves twice, once for each slip. It runs as often as a finger likes on the total cell, nothing is marked either way, and the voice says nothing at all while it happens.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase the drawn class stands along the top of the desk and the slip heap is empty. The question card asking how each child came to school sits in the slot. On the second the heap is full, and the table stands beside it with a heading cell for each answer, every number cell empty and the total cell empty. On the third the pictograph board has slid over the table, its title strip and key card showing and one row lit. On the fourth the same board stands with every row's number written, the compare rail empty under it and the total bar waiting at the left. The running count at the top left holds what this phase has done so far against what it holds, and the answer slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once, while the voice asks its question: the first child in the class row, or the top slip of the heap, or the lit row, or the largest row's number, gives one slow pulse. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any class of up to thirty children and any question put to them, with the table, the pictograph board, the compare rail and the total bar all open. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on what data is, setting data out in a table and finding its total, reading a pictograph row with its key, and finding the most, the least, the same and the total.
voiceLines: A class along the top, and an empty table on the desk. Ask each child.
Ask each child. What can all these answers tell the school?
Where does this answer belong? Now add the columns. Does the total match the heap?
Count the pictures in this row. What does one picture stand for?
Which is the most? Which is the least? Which two are the same? Now add them all.
Another question. Read the names before you read the numbers.
Free play. Any class and any question, with the table and the board open.
Read the name at the top of the column, and count that row again.
Answers collected, set out under their names, read with the key, and compared.

observations.why: A child who has answered cannot be asked again, and nobody was skipped.
observations.soWhat: Data is collected one fact at a time, and each fact carries the name of what it is.
observations.observe: Every child in the class row gave one slip, and the heap's count matched the children asked.

observations.why: Adding the columns counts every slip once, and a child who gave two answers put two slips in the heap.
observations.soWhat: A table's numbers add up to the children when each child gave one answer, and to the answers otherwise.
observations.observe: The total cell matched the heap of slips every time, and the heap matched the class when each child gave one answer.

observations.why: Each symbol stood for six mangoes, so six was taken once under each symbol.
observations.soWhat: A pictograph row is its symbols counted and the key taken that many times.
observations.observe: The row reader counted five symbols into the corner, and thirty landed at the row's end.

observations.why: The rail puts the rows in order by their numbers, so equal numbers take the same place.
observations.soWhat: The most, the least and the same are read from the numbers, and how many more is the smaller taken from the larger.
observations.observe: Two numbers shared one place on the rail, and the most and the least stood at its two ends.

phases.screen: a drawn class along the top of the desk, an empty heap and a question card asking how each child came to school
phases.win: the last slip lands and the question card turns to show what the heap tells
phases.traceback: Every answer drops into the tray, the slips gather under their names with a count for each, and the desk shows what the facts tell.
ladder: Each slip names a colour. What could the class learn from the heap?
Line up the four counts. Which number is the biggest?
What does the drawing count, and what is its name?
Read each name with its count. What do they tell you?
A fact gives information when its name says what it counts. Look again.

phases.screen: the heap of slips beside a ruled table with a heading for each answer and every number cell empty
phases.win: the heap empties into the columns and the total cell matches the number of slips collected
phases.traceback: Every card goes under its heading; the numbers are added one at a time into the total cell, or taken one at a time from the whole into the empty cell.
ladder: The four names are seasons, not children. Add the numbers under them.
Every child is counted under one fruit. Take each fruit's number once.
The whole class is 30. Which part is left after the games you know?
Each child is counted once in the table. Which numbers are the parts of the group?
The parts add up to the whole group.

phases.screen: the pictograph board over the table, with its title strip and key card, and one row lit
phases.win: the key's value is taken once for each symbol and the row's number lands at the end of the row
phases.traceback: The key is taken once under every picture, climbing to the row's number, which lands in the row's tag.
ladder: One picture is not one mango. What does the key say?
Each picture holds more than one pencil. Use the key for every picture.
Read each day's row on its own, with the key.
Look at the key card. How many does one picture hold?
Count on by the key's number, once for each picture.

phases.screen: the pictograph board with every row's number written, the compare rail empty and the total bar waiting
phases.win: the rows stand in order on the rail, two equal numbers level with each other, and the total fills the bar
phases.traceback: The rows' numbers go into the total bar and are added one at a time, or stand in order on the compare rail, or are read with the key; the answer is banded.
ladder: Add the rows' numbers, not the stars.
Look at the two ends of the rail. Which end holds the smallest number?
Find the longest row, then read it with the key.
Read each row's number first. Which numbers does the question need?
Compare the numbers for most and least. Add every row once for the total.

onWrong.marks: Nothing is marked, nothing resets, no colour means good or bad. The child's answer stays; the pad re-opens after the traceback.
tracebacks: Phase 1: Every answer drops into the tray, the slips gather under their names with a count for each, and the desk shows what the facts tell.
Phase 2: Every card goes under its heading; the numbers are added one at a time into the total cell, or taken one at a time from the whole into the empty cell.
Phase 3: The key is taken once under every picture, climbing to the row's number, which lands in the row's tag.
Phase 4: The rows' numbers go into the total bar and are added one at a time, or stand in order on the compare rail, or are read with the key; the answer is banded.

voice.opening: A class stands along the top of the desk, with a tray for their answers.
voice.onMiss: the item's own miss line, then the phase's two ladder rungs
voice.onFinish: Answers collected, set out under their names, read with the key, and compared.
voice.rules: Spoken on opening, as each phase begins, on each question, on a miss and on the summary page. Every line is printed in the bubble, numbers as words, by the device's own voice (Indian English first). Muting keeps the child's place; unmuting speaks on from the word it reached. If the browser refuses speech until a tap, the first line waits behind a Tap to start cover.

guide.playsOn: none: an Udgam tool opens straight on its phase; the phase's teach lines are spoken first, and a demo phase waits for the child's own act.

palette.rule: A content colour fills countable things only and chrome never borrows one; coloured numerals and words take a deeper ink of their colour (4.5:1).

items.planQuestion: A class writes down each child's favourite colour. Is the list of answers data?

question.en: A class writes down each child's favourite colour. Is the list of answers data?

items.planAnswer: Yes. It is a collection of facts that gives useful information: which colours the class likes

items.planQuestion: A librarian writes down how many children in each of four classes have a library card: Class 4A 23, Class 4B 31, Class 4C 18 and Class 4D 27. Is this data, and what can it tell the librarian?

question.en: A librarian writes down how many children in each of four classes have a library card. Tap each class for its count. What can this data tell the librarian? Which class has the most card holders?

items.planAnswer: Yes, it is data. It tells that Class 4B has the most card holders, 31, and that 99 children have a card in all

items.planQuestion: Which of these is data: the number of rainy days in each month of last year, or a drawing of a rain cloud?

question.en: One card counts the rainy days in each month of last year. The other is a drawing of a rain cloud. Which of these is data?

items.planAnswer: The number of rainy days in each month, because those are facts collected to give useful information

items.planQuestion: Children in a class chose their favourite season. Summer was chosen by 6 children, the rainy season by 9, winter by 8 and spring by 5. Each child chose one season. Set this out in a table and find how many children there are.

question.en: Children in a class chose their favourite season. Summer was chosen by 6 children, the rainy season by 9, winter by 8 and spring by 5. Each child chose one season. Set this out in a table and find how many children there are.

items.planAnswer: A table with Summer 6, Rainy season 9, Winter 8 and Spring 5, and 28 children in all

items.planQuestion: A table of the fruit children chose shows mango 7, guava 5, banana 9 and apple 4. Each child chose one fruit. How many children chose a fruit?

question.en: A table of the fruit children chose shows mango 7, guava 5, banana 9 and apple 4. How many children chose a fruit?

items.planQuestion: A class of 30 set out its favourite games in a table: kabaddi 8, cricket 11, football 6, and the cell for kho-kho left empty. Each child chose one game. What number goes in the kho-kho cell?

question.en: A class of 30 set out its favourite games in a table. Kabaddi has 8, cricket 11, football 6, and the kho-kho cell is empty. Everyone picked only one game. What number goes in the kho-kho cell?

ask.en: What goes in the kho-kho cell?

items.planQuestion: A pictograph titled Mangoes Picked has the key one mango picture for 6 mangoes. The row for the tallest tree holds 5 mango pictures. How many mangoes were picked from that tree?

question.en: A pictograph titled Mangoes Picked has the key one mango picture for 6 mangoes. The row for the tallest tree holds 5 mango pictures. How many mangoes were picked from that tree?

items.planQuestion: In a pictograph of pencils sold, one pencil picture stands for 10 pencils. A row holds 7 pencil pictures. How many pencils is that?

question.en: In a pictograph of pencils sold, one pencil picture stands for 10 pencils. A row holds 7 pencil pictures. How many pencils is that?

items.planQuestion: A pictograph of glasses of juice sold has the key one glass picture for 8 glasses. The rows for three days hold 2, 5 and 4 glass pictures. How many glasses were sold on each day?

question.en: A pictograph of glasses of juice sold has the key one glass picture for 8 glasses. The rows for three days hold 2, 5 and 4 glass pictures. How many glasses were sold on each day?

items.planQuestion: A pictograph of stickers collected by four classes has the key one star for 4 stickers. Class 4A has 5 stars, 4B has 8, 4C has 3 and 4D has 5. Which class collected the most, which the fewest, which two collected the same, and how many stickers were collected in all?

question.en: A pictograph of stickers collected by four classes has the key one star for 4 stickers. Class 4A has 5 stars, 4B has 8, 4C has 3 and 4D has 5. Drag each row's number into the bar. How many stickers were collected in all?

items.planAnswer: 4B the most, 32 stickers; 4C the fewest, 12; 4A and 4D the same, 20 each; 84 stickers in all

items.planQuestion: A canteen sold 14 plates of idli on Monday, 9 on Tuesday, 14 on Wednesday and 11 on Thursday. On which day were the fewest sold, which two days sold the same, and how many plates were sold in all?

question.en: A canteen sold 14 plates of idli on Monday, 9 on Tuesday, 14 on Wednesday and 11 on Thursday. Stand each day's number on the rail. On which day were the fewest plates sold?

items.planAnswer: Tuesday the fewest; Monday and Wednesday the same, 14 each; 48 plates in all

items.planQuestion: In a pictograph of trees planted by four houses, one tree picture stands for 5 trees. Ganga has 6 pictures, Yamuna 4, Kaveri 9 and Narmada 4. Which house planted the most trees, how many is that, and how many trees were planted in all?

question.en: In a pictograph of trees planted by four houses, one tree picture stands for 5 trees. Ganga has 6 pictures, Yamuna 4, Kaveri 9 and Narmada 4. Find the house that planted the most trees. How many trees did it plant?

items.planAnswer: Kaveri, 45 trees; 115 trees in all, because 30 + 20 + 45 + 20 = 115

scoring.wrong: costs nothing, never marked, counted only for first try accuracy
scoring.stars: one for finishing, two at sixty per cent right first time, three at ninety; hidden with the first-try line by showScore false
scoring.phaseMount: a mount scores every phase it plays, from its phase to the last (+5 a question; phases of 3, 3, 3, 3 questions)
scoring.finishCard: stars and the Right first time line under the phase rows on the summary page

hostContract.phase: absent (not a finite number): the whole lesson, phases one to 4 in a row, the summary page at the end, finished once. Present: rounded and clamped to one to 4; the tool starts at that phase and, as the NCERT tools do, walks on by itself after each phase's last question (its closing line, then 1.4 s), in user and AI mode alike, through phase 4 to the summary page; finished once, from the summary page.
hostContract.navigableDots: true (or no phase): user mode, the phase dots are controls; otherwise AI mode, the dots show progress and the agent drives window.toolApi.

onProgress.done: questions right so far in this phase

hostContract.emits: every event is dispatched on window and, when framed, posted to window.parent as { type: 'event', name, detail }

terminalEvent.fires: once per mount, from the summary page after the last phase, 5 s after the page opens (its lines may still be going on); one-shot guarded and re-armed by restart or Play again; never sent at the end of an earlier phase (the tool walks on), and never if Free play or Play again is tapped first
